questions.primaryUnit: Unit 1: Exploring One-Variable Data and Collecting Data
questions.secondaryUnit: Unit 2: Probability, Random Variables, and Probability Distributions
questions.prompt:
A university wants to estimate the proportion of its 6,000 commuter students who parked in an unauthorized campus area at least once during the previous month. Because the question is sensitive, the university takes a simple random sample of 300 commuter students and uses the following randomized-response procedure.

Each participating student privately rolls a fair six-sided die and does not reveal the result.

Die result 1 or 2: Answer “Yes.”
Die result 3 or 4: Answer “No.”
Die result 5 or 6: Answer the parking question truthfully.

Of the 300 selected students, 270 participate. Among the participants, 119 answer “Yes.”

(a) Identify the population, intended sample, respondent sample, and population parameter of interest.

(b) State a statistical question that the study is designed to answer. Describe how the university could select the original simple random sample from a complete commuter-student roster.

(c) Let p be the true proportion of commuter students who parked in an unauthorized area, and let q be the probability that a participant answers “Yes” under the procedure. Show that q = 1/3 + p/3. Explain how the procedure provides privacy.

(d) Use the observed responses to estimate p. Interpret the estimate in context.

(e) Explain why the randomized-response mechanism can reduce response bias but does not eliminate possible nonresponse bias. State a reasonable follow-up action.
questions.scoringGuide:
Total Points: 10
(a) 2 points
· Point 1: Identifies the population as all 6,000 commuter students, the intended sample as the 300 selected students, and the respondent sample as the 270 participants.
· Point 2: Defines p as the true proportion of all 6,000 commuter students who parked in an unauthorized campus area at least once during the previous month.
(b) 2 points
· Point 1: States a question about the proportion or percentage of the university's commuter students who parked in an unauthorized area at least once during the previous month.
· Point 2: Describes a valid SRS method, such as assigning distinct labels 0001 through 6000 and using a random-number generator to select 300 distinct labels without replacement.
(c) 2 points
· Point 1: Derives q = P(forced Yes) + P(truthful branch and true Yes) = 1/3 + (1/3)p.
· Point 2: Explains that either response can result from the die mechanism or from truthful reporting, so the researcher cannot determine an individual student's parking behavior from the response alone.
(d) 2 points
· Point 1: Calculates q̂ = 119/270 ≈ 0.4407 and p̂ = 3q̂ − 1 ≈ 0.3222.
· Point 2: Interprets the estimate as approximately 32.2% of the university's commuter students having parked in an unauthorized area at least once during the previous month, subject to the study's limitations.
(e) 2 points
· Point 1: Explains that privacy may encourage more truthful responses, but the 30 nonparticipants could have a different unauthorized-parking rate, so randomized response does not remove nonresponse bias.
· Point 2: Proposes a reasonable action such as repeated confidential contact, varied contact times or modes, or a short nonresponse follow-up while preserving the randomized-response protocol.
questions.modelResponse:
The intended sample consists of everyone selected, whereas the respondent sample consists only of those who participated. The die creates known random noise: one-third of participants are forced to say Yes, one-third are forced to say No, and one-third answer truthfully. Thus, q = 1/3 + p/3, so the parking proportion is estimated by 3q̂ − 1, not by the raw Yes proportion.

With q̂ = 119/270, the estimated parking proportion is about 0.322. The randomized mechanism protects individual privacy and can reduce deliberate misreporting. It cannot make the 270 respondents representative of the 30 nonrespondents, so confidential follow-up is still important.

questions.secondaryUnit: Unit 1: Exploring One-Variable Data and Collecting Data
questions.prompt:
An environmental team studies the relationship between streamside tree-canopy cover and midsummer water temperature at 10 monitoring sites in one watershed. For each site, x is the percentage of the stream segment covered by tree canopy and y is the mean afternoon water temperature, in degrees Celsius, during the monitoring week.

Site       A     B     C     D     E     F     G     H     I     J
x (%)     10    20    25    35    45    55    60    70    80    90
y (°C)  25.1  23.0  24.2  21.8  22.5  19.8  21.2  18.5  19.3  16.9

Least-squares output for predicting temperature from canopy cover is

ŷ = 25.756 − 0.09236x
r = −0.947
r² = 0.896

(a) Sketch a scatterplot with correctly labeled axes and an appropriate scale. Describe the form, direction, strength, and any unusual features of the relationship.

(b) For Site G, calculate the predicted temperature and residual. Interpret the sign of the residual in context.

(c) Interpret the slope and r² in context.

(d) According to the fitted line, determine the minimum whole-number canopy percentage needed for a predicted mean afternoon temperature of at most 19°C. Explain whether this use is interpolation or extrapolation.

(e) A watershed manager claims that increasing any site's canopy cover to the percentage found in part (d) will cause its mean afternoon temperature to be at most 19°C. Evaluate the claim using the data and study design.
questions.scoringGuide:
Total Points: 10
(a) 2 points
· Point 1: Sketches a scatterplot with canopy cover on the horizontal axis, temperature on the vertical axis, suitable scales, and all 10 points plotted consistently with the table.
· Point 2: Describes a strong, negative, roughly linear relationship with some scatter and no clearly isolated unusual point.
(b) 2 points
· Point 1: Calculates ŷ = 25.756 − 0.09236(60) ≈ 20.214°C and residual = 21.2 − 20.214 ≈ 0.986°C.
· Point 2: Interprets the positive residual to mean that Site G was about 0.99°C warmer than the model predicted for a site with 60% canopy cover.
(c) 2 points
· Point 1: Interprets the slope: each additional percentage point of canopy cover is associated with a predicted decrease of about 0.092°C in mean afternoon water temperature, on average.
· Point 2: Interprets r² = 0.896 as 89.6% of the variation in mean afternoon temperature among these sites being explained by the linear relationship with canopy-cover percentage.
(d) 2 points
· Point 1: Solves 25.756 − 0.09236x ≤ 19 to obtain x ≥ about 73.14%, and therefore selects 74% as the minimum whole-number percentage.
· Point 2: Identifies the calculation as interpolation because 74% lies within the observed canopy range of 10% to 90%.
(e) 2 points
· Point 1: Explains that the line predicts an average response and does not guarantee that every site at 74% canopy has a temperature at or below 19°C, as shown by nonzero residual variation.
· Point 2: Rejects the causal wording because canopy cover was observed rather than randomly assigned and identifies a plausible confounder, such as stream depth, flow, elevation, or channel width, that could affect temperature and be associated with canopy.
questions.modelResponse:
The plotted points should descend from upper left to lower right in a nearly linear pattern. At 60% canopy, the model predicts about 20.214°C; the observed 21.2°C is higher, so the residual is positive. The slope describes an association per percentage point, and r² describes explained variation in the response—not the percentage of sites lying on the line.

Solving the fitted equation gives a threshold just above 73%, so the minimum whole-number model setting is 74%. That value is inside the data range. Still, predicted means are not guarantees for individual sites, and an observational relationship cannot establish that changing canopy alone causes the temperature difference.

questions.primaryUnit: Unit 3: Inference for Categorical Data: Proportions
questions.secondaryUnit: Unit 1: Exploring One-Variable Data and Collecting Data
questions.prompt:
A public-library system has 12,000 members whose accounts have been inactive for at least one year. The system takes a simple random sample of 600 such members and randomly assigns 300 to receive a personalized reactivation message and 300 to receive a standard message. A member is classified as reactivated if the member borrows at least one item during the next 30 days.

Message type       Reactivated    Not reactivated    Total
Personalized             84              216          300
Standard                 63              237          300

At the α = 0.05 significance level, test whether the personalized message produces a higher reactivation proportion than the standard message.

(a) Define the population proportions and state the null and alternative hypotheses.

(b) Identify the appropriate inference procedure and check its conditions.

(c) Calculate the sample proportions, pooled proportion, standard error, test statistic, and p-value.

(d) State a conclusion in context using α = 0.05, including the appropriate scope of inference.

(e) Describe a Type I error in context.
questions.scoringGuide:
Total Points: 10
(a) 2 points
· Point 1: Defines pP and pS as the true reactivation proportions for all 12,000 inactive members if sent the personalized and standard messages, respectively.
· Point 2: States H0: pP − pS = 0 and Ha: pP − pS > 0.
(b) 3 points
· Point 1: Selects a one-sided two-proportion z test.
· Point 2: Cites the original SRS, random assignment to two separate groups, and the 10% condition because 600 ≤ 0.10(12,000) = 1,200.
· Point 3: Checks the pooled large-count condition using expected counts 300(0.245) = 73.5 reactivated and 300(0.755) = 226.5 not reactivated in each group, all at least 10.
(c) 3 points
· Point 1: Calculates p̂P = 84/300 = 0.280, p̂S = 63/300 = 0.210, observed difference 0.070, and pooled p̂ = 147/600 = 0.245.
· Point 2: Calculates SE0 = √[0.245(0.755)(1/300 + 1/300)] ≈ 0.03512 and z = 0.070/0.03512 ≈ 1.99.
· Point 3: Calculates the one-sided p-value P(Z ≥ 1.99) ≈ 0.0231.
(d) 1 point
· Point 1: Because 0.0231 < 0.05, rejects H0 and concludes that there is convincing evidence that the personalized message causes a higher reactivation proportion than the standard message for the population of 12,000 inactive members, with causation supported by random assignment and generalization supported by the SRS.
(e) 1 point
· Point 1: Describes a Type I error as concluding that the personalized message produces a higher reactivation proportion when, in truth, the two message types have equal reactivation proportions for the population.
questions.modelResponse:
This is a comparison of two independent treatment proportions. The null model uses one common proportion, so the standard error for the test must use the pooled estimate 147/600 = 0.245. Random sampling supports population generalization, and random assignment supports a causal comparison of the two message types.

The observed advantage is 0.070, producing z ≈ 1.99 and a one-sided p-value of about 0.0231. At α = 0.05, the null hypothesis is rejected. A Type I error would mean asserting a real personalized-message advantage even though no population treatment difference exists.

questions.primaryUnit: Unit 2: Probability, Random Variables, and Probability Distributions
questions.secondaryUnit: Unit 4: Inference for Quantitative Data: Means
questions.prompt:
A packaging machine fills more than 1,000 snack pouches each hour. When the process is operating as intended, individual fill masses are independent and Normally distributed with mean 250 grams and standard deviation 12 grams. The standard deviation remains 12 grams even if the process mean shifts.

Under the current monitoring rule, an independent random sample of 36 pouches is selected each hour. The machine is stopped for inspection if the sample mean fill mass is less than 246 grams.

(a) When the process mean is 250 grams, describe the sampling distribution of the sample mean and calculate the probability that the rule stops the machine. Interpret this probability as a false-alarm rate.

(b) Suppose the process mean has shifted to 245 grams. Calculate the probability that the current rule stops the machine and the probability that it misses the shift during a given hour.

(c) A supervisor says, “Because the false-alarm probability is only about 2.3%, about 97.7% of all stop alerts must indicate a real shift.” Evaluate this statement.

(d) A proposed rule uses a sample of 64 pouches. Determine the cutoff c for stopping when x̄ < c so that the false-alarm probability remains approximately 0.0228. Then calculate the probability that the proposed rule detects a shift to 245 grams.

(e) Compare the current and proposed rules. Recommend one rule and justify the recommendation using statistical evidence, operational cost, and the model assumptions.
questions.scoringGuide:
Total Points: 10
(a) 2 points
· Point 1: States that, when μ = 250, x̄ is Normal with mean 250 grams and standard deviation 12/√36 = 2 grams.
· Point 2: Calculates P(x̄ < 246) = P(Z < −2) ≈ 0.0228 and interprets it as about a 2.28% chance of an unnecessary stop in an hour when the process mean is on target.
(b) 2 points
· Point 1: When μ = 245, calculates P(x̄ < 246) = P(Z < 0.50) ≈ 0.6915 as the hourly detection probability.
· Point 2: Calculates 1 − 0.6915 = 0.3085 and interprets it as the probability that the current rule fails to stop during an hour when the true mean is 245 grams.
(c) 2 points
· Point 1: Rejects the statement because 0.0228 is P(alert | no shift), whereas the supervisor is making a claim about P(shift | alert), which reverses the conditioning.
· Point 2: Explains that the proportion of alerts corresponding to real shifts also depends on how frequently process shifts occur, information that is not provided.
(d) 2 points
· Point 1: Uses the new standard deviation 12/√64 = 1.5 and z = −2 to obtain c = 250 − 2(1.5) = 247 grams.
· Point 2: When μ = 245, calculates P(x̄ < 247) = P[Z < (247 − 245)/1.5] = P(Z < 1.33) ≈ 0.9088.
(e) 2 points
· Point 1: Gives an evidence-based comparison: both rules have about the same 2.28% false-alarm rate, but the proposed rule increases detection probability from about 0.6915 to 0.9088 and reduces the miss probability.
· Point 2: Gives a justified recommendation that weighs the proposed rule's improved detection against the cost of inspecting 64 rather than 36 pouches and notes reliance on random independent sampling, approximate Normal behavior, and a stable 12-gram standard deviation.
questions.modelResponse:
The sample mean has standard deviation σ/√n. For n = 36, the standard error is 2 grams, so a 246-gram cutoff is two standard errors below the on-target mean and gives a false-alarm probability of 0.0228. If the process shifts to 245 grams, the same cutoff is 0.5 standard error above the new mean, giving detection probability 0.6915 and miss probability 0.3085.

The supervisor reverses a conditional probability: a low false-alarm rate does not determine the percentage of alerts that are true without a process-shift base rate. With n = 64, a cutoff of 247 grams preserves the z = −2 false-alarm boundary while raising detection probability for μ = 245 to about 0.9088. The larger-sample rule has better statistical performance for that shift, but a recommendation should also account for inspection cost and whether the Normal, independence, and constant-variability assumptions are credible.
